title: Day-to-day coupling instability is a resilience marker that predicts clinical burden
statement: The day-to-day variability (instability) of glucose-HR coupling strength is itself a marker of physiological resilience. In healthy individuals, coupling strength varies substantially from day to day because it is context-dependent (meals, activity, sleep quality, stress). In advanced diabetes, coupling becomes rigidly positive every day (loss of context dependence), reducing day-to-day variability. The coefficient of variation (CV) of daily glucose-HR coupling across the 10-day window decreases with diabetes severity and independently predicts frailty index and allostatic load.
mechanism: Day-to-day variability in inter-organ coupling reflects the system's capacity to modulate its internal coordination in response to varying daily demands. In healthy physiology, autonomic reflexes and metabolic flexibility allow glucose-HR coupling to be strong on some days (high carb intake, sedentary) and weak or negative on others (exercise days, fasting). This variability is a signature of adaptive capacity. In diabetes, loss of metabolic flexibility (impaired fuel switching), autonomic rigidity (fixed sympathetic dominance), and reduced behavioral variability (less exercise, more routine) collapse the coupling into a narrow, persistently positive range. This loss of day-to-day coupling variability parallels the loss-of-complexity principle from Lipsitz & Goldberger: disease reduces not just signal complexity but also the variability of inter-signal relationships.
predictions: The CV of daily glucose-HR coupling (computed from ~10 daily estimates per person) decreases with diabetes severity (d > 0.25)
Day-to-day coupling CV independently predicts frailty index (partial r > 0.08) after adjusting for age, site, HbA1c, BMI, and mean coupling level
Day-to-day coupling CV independently predicts allostatic load (partial r > 0.08) after the same adjustment
Negative control: the CV of daily glucose MEAN does not have the same independent predictive power (variability of coupling, not of glucose level, is the marker)
Participants with the lowest day-to-day coupling CV have the highest coupling means (rigid positive coupling = low variability + high mean)

literature.title: Loss of 'complexity' and aging: potential applications of fractals and chaos theory to senescence
literature.key_finding: Aging and disease reduce physiological complexity across multiple scales and systems.
literature.relevance: The foundational principle that disease reduces variability/complexity, extended from single-signal complexity to inter-signal coupling variability.

literature.title: Disruption of multisystem responses to stress in type 2 diabetes
literature.key_finding: T2D shows attenuated stress reactivity and recovery across multiple systems, consistent with reduced adaptive capacity.
literature.relevance: Supports the idea that diabetes reduces the variability of physiological responses, which should manifest as reduced day-to-day coupling variability.

literature.title: From frailty to resilience: exploring adaptive capacity and reserve in older adults
literature.key_finding: Resilience in aging is the ability to recover from perturbations, and loss of resilience precedes overt functional decline.
literature.relevance: Frames day-to-day coupling variability as a resilience metric that may detect pre-clinical regulatory failure.

feasibility.statistical_power: N~1900; computing per-day coupling from ~288 points/day, then CV across ~10 days per person
key_challenges: Only ~10 days limits precision of CV estimates; some days may have missing data
Day-to-day coupling CV may partly reflect CGM sensor artifacts or HR data gaps
Need to separate genuine physiological variability from measurement noise
dataset_limitations: 10-day window provides only ~8-10 independent daily estimates for CV computation
Daily activities are not logged; day-to-day behavioral variability is unmeasured
Cross-sectional: cannot determine whether low CV precedes or follows clinical burden

test_plan.primary_method: Compute per-day glucose-HR correlation for each participant's 10-day window, then compute CV of daily correlations. Test group trend and partial correlations with clinical outcomes.
implementation_steps: Step 1: Segment each participant's aligned glucose-HR data into calendar days (midnight to midnight, local time)
Step 2: Compute Pearson correlation between glucose and HR for each day (require >= 100 valid 5-min points per day, i.e., >8.3 hours)
Step 3: Compute per-person statistics: mean daily coupling, SD daily coupling, CV daily coupling, number of valid days
Step 4: Filter to participants with >= 7 valid days
Step 5: Test group differences in CV of daily coupling across severity groups
Step 6: Fit partial correlation models: CV ~ frailty_index, adjusting for age, site, HbA1c, BMI, mean_coupling
Step 7: Negative control: compute CV of daily glucose mean and test same partial correlations
Step 8: Test correlation between mean coupling and coupling CV (expected negative: high mean = low variability)
test_plan.time_window: Per-day within 10-day window (then aggregated to per-person CV)
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Cohen's d 0.25-0.40 for CV group trend; partial r 0.08-0.12 for CV vs frailty/allostatic load
test_plan.success_criterion: Coupling CV decreases with severity (FDR p < 0.01) and independently predicts frailty/allostatic load after adjustment for HbA1c, BMI, and mean coupling level
test_plan.refutation_criterion: No group difference in coupling CV. CV does not predict frailty/allostatic load after adjusting for mean coupling level. CV of daily glucose mean is an equally good predictor (coupling-specific variability is not special).
sensitivity_checks: Use MAD (median absolute deviation) instead of SD for robust variability estimation
Compute coupling CV for awake-only periods to avoid sleep artifact
Split first 5 days vs last 5 days to assess stability of the CV metric itself
Test rolling 3-day windows instead of calendar days
Bootstrap per-person CV estimates by resampling daily values
secondary_methods: Shannon entropy of daily coupling distribution (binned)
Autocorrelation of daily coupling sequence (memory in coupling dynamics)

issues: Computing a CV from ~8-10 daily values is statistically fragile. The sampling distribution of CV from N=10 is very wide; the estimated CV has a CV of its own that is ~30%. Group differences in coupling CV will be dominated by noise in the CV estimate, not genuine physiological differences.

The prediction that 'lower CV = higher mean coupling' creates a potential statistical artifact: if coupling has a ceiling effect (bounded above), high-mean coupling mechanically has lower variance. The correlation between mean and CV may be mathematical rather than biological.

Day-to-day variability in coupling could reflect measurement noise (CGM sensor drift, HR data gaps, varying data quality across days) rather than genuine physiological variability. Without a noise model, genuine and artifactual variability are inseparable.

The 'loss of complexity' framing is borrowed from Lipsitz & Goldberger, but their framework applies to within-signal complexity (MSE of HR, fractal dimension), not to the variability of inter-signal coupling across days. Extending the concept to day-to-day coupling variability is an extrapolation, not a direct application.
confounders_missed: Data quality variability across days: days with more missing data have noisier coupling estimates, inflating apparent CV
Weekend/weekday cycling: behavioral differences between weekend and weekday create systematic (non-random) day-to-day coupling variability that is not 'resilience'
Weather and season: outdoor activity patterns change with weather, creating day-to-day behavioral variability that drives coupling variability
suggestions: Use 4h blocks within days (giving ~60 blocks per person) rather than daily estimates. This provides a more robust variability estimate with enough degrees of freedom.
Explicitly test and report the mean-CV correlation. If r(mean, CV) > 0.5, the CV is largely a mathematical consequence of the mean and not an independent metric.
Compute coupling variability from AWAKE-ONLY periods to reduce the confound of varying sleep quality across nights.
Report split-half reliability of the CV estimate (first 5 days vs last 5 days). If reliability < 0.5, the metric is too noisy to be useful.

notes: Conceptually elegant: not just 'is coupling altered' but 'is the variability of coupling altered.' Extends loss-of-complexity from single signals to inter-signal relationships. 10-day window is the main limitation.
